title: Giving as practice
hook: the first perfection lived: give something daily this week

segments.voice: Yesterday we walked around the mountain: Kailash, a kora, and a summit left unclimbed. Your line was around the mountain. What did you keep on your right? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-nine.

A bowl of rice is passed from hand to hand at dawn. A monk walks barefoot down a street, and someone kneels and spoons food into his bowl, and the monk says nothing and walks on. Neither one says thank you. That is not rudeness. The giver is not doing the monk a favor, and the monk is not doing the giver one either. Something else is happening. For the last week, this path has been on pilgrimage, walking to the places of the Buddha's life. Now it turns inward, to a different kind of road: the perfections, the qualities Buddhists say a person grows on the way to awakening. And the list begins with the simplest thing in that bowl. Today: giving as practice.
screen: `RICE INTO A BOWL AT DAWN.` → `NO THANK YOU, AND NO FAVOR.` → `THE PERFECTIONS BEGIN.`

segments.voice: First, the list. Theravada Buddhists keep one list of perfections and Mahayana Buddhists keep another. They differ in length and wording. But both begin in the same place: giving, dana. Before anything else on either list, there is the open hand. Second, the Buddha's own claim. In a short collection called the Itivuttaka, he says something startling. If people knew, as he knows, the fruit of giving and sharing, they would not eat without giving first. Even with their last bite, their last mouthful, they would not eat it without sharing, if there were someone to share it with. That's the bar he sets. Not the leftovers. The last mouthful. Third, two kinds of gift. In the same collection, the Buddha names two kinds of giving: the gift of material things, and the gift of the teaching. Bread is a gift. So is a true word at the right time. Neither needs to be large. Fourth, why it's a practice and not just a kind act. Giving loosens the grip. A verse of the Dhammapada, in Max Muller's old translation, puts it this way: "Let a man overcome anger by love, let him overcome evil by good; let him overcome the greedy by liberality, the liar by truth!" Liberality is the old word for generosity, and here it is a medicine for grasping, including one's own. So giving, to monks, to neighbors, to strangers, is not only to help, though it helps. It is a way to practice letting go, one small thing at a time. That's why nobody needs to say thank you at the bowl. The giving was the practice.
screen: `BOTH LISTS BEGIN WITH GIVING.` · `EVEN THE LAST MOUTHFUL.` · `THINGS, AND A TRUE WORD.` · then, large: `OVERCOME THE GREEDY BY LIBERALITY.`

segments.voice: If you'd like to start the week of giving now, sit, and breathe. Bring to mind the next seven days. For each one, choose one small thing you could give: a coin, a meal, a compliment, an hour, a book you've finished, a true word to someone who needs it. Don't make it big. Let each day have one gift. Then picture handing over the first one, and notice the hand opening. Rest in that open hand for the rest of the sit. The bell holds the time.
Giving as practice. Dana, the first of the perfections in both Theravada and Mahayana lists: giving not only to help, but to train the heart to let go. Today's word.
Your line: the first perfection. Today, give one thing away before you eat, even something small, and let no thank you be needed. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: Buddhists practice dana by offering food to monks and nuns, supporting temples, and giving to people in need, and in Theravada countries the morning alms round is a daily chance to give.

fork.setup: you have one last bite of food. someone beside you has none. by the Buddha's words in the Itivuttaka, what would a person who knew the fruit of giving do?
options: eat it; it's the last one.
fork.reveal: share it. he says that if people knew the fruit of giving, they would not eat even their last mouthful without sharing it, if someone were there to receive.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit dana: giving, generosity, the first of the perfections.

trapdoor: what you thought: giving is being nice.
what it means: a training in letting go, practiced daily, small or large, until the hand opens easily.
what a scholar hears: dana at the head of both the Theravada and Mahayana perfections, the Itivuttaka's last mouthful, and the gift of the teaching.

sources.quoted: Let a man overcome anger by love, let him overcome evil by good; let him overcome the greedy by liberality, the liar by truth!

notes: Dhammapada 223 quoted from Max Müller (SBE X, 1881); confirm exact wording.

Itivuttaka 26 paraphrased: if beings knew the result of giving and sharing as the Buddha knows it, they would not eat without having given, even their last morsel, if there were someone to receive it. Confirm.
Itivuttaka 98 paraphrased: two kinds of gift, material (amisa) and Dhamma; the text adds that the gift of Dhamma is foremost, which was left out. Confirm.
Theravada (ten paramis) and Mahayana (six paramitas) lists both begin with dana; counts left out per the claims rule. Confirm.
Hook: the silent alms round and 'neither one says thank you' describe Theravada custom; confirm phrasing is fair.
Hook transition looks back on the pilgrimage days (1392–1398) and opens the perfections run (1399 on).
